style_prompt:
### DIRECTOR'S NOTES
Style: Warm, natural and conversational, a documentary storyteller with bright, forward-leaning energy. Curious and quietly wondrous about how this was done: a machine drew the lakes, people checked the lines, and an open map let a small newsroom count Alaska. Careful and fair, never alarmed and never hype. A dry half-smile on the press release line. Firm up at 'Now the case for yes' and stay steady and even-handed through those numbers. Keep every routine pause short, a quick breath at the period and straight on; the one longer rest is the marked short pause right before 'A real push.', which then settles low and grounded. Close on the final question warm, open and inviting, as if asking the listener directly.
Pace: MEASURED and unhurried, never padded. THIS IS A TWO MINUTE PIECE, about one hundred and fifteen
seconds, and the read must fill it, so let every sentence land and take an easy breath at each period,
a natural beat rather than a long pause. Save real rests for the marked short pauses. Do not rush the
numbers. Vary the tone line to line so no two sentences sound the same.
Emphasis: lean on the key word in each line; let numbers land.

lines.text: A machine drew the world's glacier lakes. [short pause] Twice.
lines.why: Bright opening claim, a quick beat, then 'Twice' lands as the small wonder that pulls the viewer in.

lines.text: It read Landsat satellite pictures from about two thousand and about twenty twenty, and traced shorelines.
lines.why: Even, moving explainer of the method; drop from the hook so the setup breathes.

lines.text: Then people checked the lines by hand.
lines.why: Softer and warmer: the human check is the trust point of the celebratory angle.

lines.text: It's in Nature Climate Change, out November twentieth.
lines.why: Crisp credential, a lift back up so the citation does not sag.

lines.text: So does a lake eat its glacier?
lines.why: The question that drives the film; curious lean, rising on 'eat'.

lines.text: Worldwide, lakes touching glaciers rose by three thousand five hundred sixty-seven, about thirty-five percent.
lines.why: Let the big count land without rushing; informative, not hyped.

lines.text: But their area grew only about nine percent.
lines.why: The quiet flip: lower energy on 'only' sets up the multiplied versus swelled contrast.

lines.text: The study's press release calls Alaska's growth particularly pronounced, but prints no Alaska number.
lines.why: Half-smile carried by the notes, not a tag; the dry turn on 'no' tees up our own count.

lines.text: The authors posted their map, so we counted. Our lake count matches theirs worldwide, exactly.
lines.why: Credit to the open data, then a bright, confident 'exactly' that earns trust for what follows.

lines.text: By our count, Alaska's lakes touching glaciers went from nine hundred thirty-one to one thousand seventy-eight.
lines.why: Settle for the numbers; 'By our count' stays clear, not rushed.

lines.text: Their area grew about thirty-five percent, to about eleven hundred ninety square kilometers.
lines.why: Lift on 'area' so the ear hears area outrunning count.

lines.text: The world's lakes multiplied. Alaska's swelled.
lines.why: The film's thesis line and peak of wonder; two crisp sentences, the period alone separates them, 'swelled' lands warm and full.

lines.text: Alaska's added area alone is about half the world's, by our count, from about one in thirteen of those lakes.
lines.why: Still lit from the peak but a notch down; let 'half' and 'one in thirteen' land.

lines.text: Our count's biggest Alaska gain was Vitus Lake, at the foot of Bering Glacier. About a hundred five square kilometers became a hundred fifty-eight.
lines.why: A concrete place, told like a storyteller pointing at the map; even and grounded.

lines.text: Now the case for yes. Glaciers ending in a lake lost about sixty-six centimeters of water a year, on average. On land, about forty.
lines.why: The turn: firmer and more deliberate, giving the counterpoint full strength.

lines.text: Tobias Bolch, a co-author at TU Graz, says contact with a lake further accelerates the loss of ice.
lines.why: Measured attribution, names clean, weight on 'accelerates'.

lines.text: Then the team's machine learning models weighed the factors.
lines.why: Quiet hinge into the split; low so the next numbers can rise.

lines.text: For lake-ending glaciers worldwide, the lake explained about eleven percent of the ice loss. Climate, about forty-three. The glacier's own shape, about forty-six. [short pause]
lines.why: Three numbers in a clean list, no rush; the trailing short pause is the one longer rest of the read, placed after words so it is never line-initial.

lines.text: A real push. The smallest of the three.
lines.why: The line I most want to land: after the one longer rest, low and grounded, fair to both sides.

lines.text: The release and abstract give no split for Alaska. Here, the push could be bigger, or smaller.
lines.why: Honest open question; a slight lift on 'Here' and even weight on bigger and smaller.

lines.text: The map stops at about twenty twenty. [curious] Who traces the next one?
lines.why: Warm, direct, inviting close; [curious] mid-line after a period lifts the final question.
